---
title: "00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof"
---

## A bug that testing cannot find

Here is a situation every competitive programmer recognizes. You are solving a
problem about an array, you notice a pattern in the samples, you code the
pattern, and you get *Wrong answer on test 7*. The implementation is perfect.
The pattern was false.

Now compare that with a different failure. You reduce the problem to "find the
smallest $x$ with $Kx \equiv -S \pmod N$", you call your extended-Euclid
routine, and you get *Wrong answer on test 3* because a solution exists only
when $\gcd(K,N)$ divides $S$ — a condition you never checked, because nobody
told you it was there.

Both bugs have the same cause: a claim was used without being proved, and the
claim was false or incomplete. No amount of stress testing reliably finds
these, because the wrong claim is usually right on small cases; that is
precisely why it looked convincing.

This chapter is about the small set of habits that catch such bugs *before*
you write code: saying exactly what you are claiming, knowing which direction
of an "if and only if" you actually need, proving that a loop makes progress,
and counting a set of objects in two different ways to check yourself. None of
it requires a mathematics degree. All of it is the working language of every
later chapter.

## Prerequisites and learning objectives

You need arithmetic with integers and fractions, and nothing else. The
[notation reference](../NOTATION.qmd) collects conventions used throughout the
book.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- read a quantified statement ("for every … there exists …") and say precisely
  what a counterexample to it would look like;
- pick a proof technique — direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction —
  for a claim, and know why each one is valid;
- state an invariant for a process and use it to prove that a target state is
  unreachable, or a potential function to prove that a loop ends;
- derive Bézout's identity from Euclid's algorithm and use it to decide when
  $ax + by = c$ has integer solutions and what *all* of them are;
- justify a counting formula by exhibiting a bijection or by counting one set
  in two ways.

If all of this is familiar, skim the section headings and jump to the
exercises; they are designed to locate gaps rather than to gatekeep.

## The vocabulary, in one page

Mathematical writing is terse mostly because the same handful of symbols
appear everywhere. Here they are, with the reading you should hear in your
head.

**Sets.** $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, and $\mathbb R$ are the integers, the
rationals (fractions $p/q$ of integers with $q \ne 0$), and the reals.
$\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ is the nonnegative integers. A *set* is an unordered
collection with no repeats — think `std::set`, not `std::vector`; a *sequence*
has order and may repeat. The empty set is $\varnothing$, and $|S|$ is the
number of elements of a finite $S$.

**Index ranges.** $[0,n)$ means the integers $0, 1, \ldots, n-1$, the same
half-open convention as a C++ loop. An indexed sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i$ has
one term per index in that range.

**Empty things.** An empty sum is $0$ and an empty product is $1$. These are
not arbitrary: they are the values that make recurrences correct at size zero,
exactly as an accumulator is initialized to the identity of its operation. In
the same spirit, there is exactly one empty sequence, so a formula counting
sequences should return $1$, not $0$, at size zero. Off-by-one errors in
combinatorics are almost always disagreements about this convention.

**Functions.** $f : A \to B$ assigns one output in $B$ to each input in $A$.
It is *injective* when different inputs give different outputs (no
collisions), *surjective* when every element of $B$ is hit, and *bijective*
when both hold. A bijection between finite sets is a perfect matching between
their elements, so it proves $|A| = |B|$ — the single most useful proof
technique in counting.

**Indicators.** $[P]$ is $1$ when the proposition $P$ is true and $0$
otherwise. For instance $\sum_{i=1}^{10} [\,2 \mid i\,] = 5$. Indicators let
you move a condition out of the range of a sum and into the summand, which is
often what unlocks an algebraic simplification.

**Divisibility and floors.** $a \mid b$ ("$a$ divides $b$") means $b = ak$ for
some integer $k$; its negation is $a \nmid b$. The floor $\lfloor x \rfloor$
is the greatest integer at most $x$. Note $\lfloor -3/2 \rfloor = -2$, while
C++ integer division gives $-1$: floor rounds down, the language truncates
toward zero. Every chapter that uses floors means the mathematical one.

## Logic: what exactly must be proved?

A surprising amount of contest debugging is really the discovery that you
proved a different statement from the one you needed.

$P \Rightarrow Q$ means: every instance satisfying $P$ also satisfies $Q$. Its
*converse* $Q \Rightarrow P$ is a genuinely different claim, and one of the
two can hold while the other fails. $P \Longleftrightarrow Q$ asserts both.

This matters constantly in reductions. When you say "the answer is yes exactly
when the graph has a perfect matching", you have made two claims: a yes-instance
gives a matching, and a matching gives a yes-instance. Skipping the second is
how you end up counting configurations that do not correspond to anything.

::: {.callout-warning title="Worked failure: a necessary condition is not a solution"}
If a positive integer is divisible by $6$, then it is divisible by $3$. The
converse fails at $n = 3$.

Practically: a necessary condition is a *filter*. It can prove an instance
impossible, and that is valuable — checking parity or a gcd condition first
can save an entire wrong approach. But passing the filter does not build a
solution, and a solution written as "check the condition, then output yes" is
correct only if you also proved sufficiency.
:::

**Quantifiers.** $\forall$ is "for every" and $\exists$ is "there exists".
Their order is not decoration. "For every integer $x$ there exists an integer
$y > x$" is true. Swap the quantifiers — "there exists an integer $y$ that is
larger than every integer $x$" — and it is false. When reading a problem
statement, note which quantity is allowed to depend on which; the dependency
order is usually the whole difficulty of the problem.

To disprove a $\forall$ statement, exhibit one counterexample. To negate
"for every $x$ there exists $y$ with $P(x,y)$", say "there exists an $x$ such
that every $y$ fails $P(x,y)$" — negation flips each quantifier and negates
the inside. Doing this mechanically is useful: the negation tells you exactly
what a counterexample must look like, which is what your brute-force checker
should search for.

**Contrapositive and contradiction.** The contrapositive of $P \Rightarrow Q$
is $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$, and the two are equivalent — if $P$ forced $Q$,
then failing $Q$ rules out $P$. Sometimes one direction is far easier to argue.
To show that $n^2$ even forces $n$ even, assume instead that $n$ is odd, write
$n = 2k+1$, and compute $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, which is odd. A proof by
*contradiction* assumes the claim false and derives an impossibility; it is the
right tool when the negation gives you something concrete to manipulate.

## Induction: writing a correctness recurrence

Induction is the proof technique that most resembles code you already write.
To prove a statement $P(n)$ for every $n \ge n_0$:

1. prove the **base case** $P(n_0)$;
2. prove the **step** $P(n) \Rightarrow P(n+1)$.

The base starts a chain, and the step propagates it to every index. In *strong*
induction the step may assume $P(k)$ for all valid $k < n$, which is the exact
analogue of a dynamic program reading every smaller state. In fact the
correspondence is precise: a DP is correct when its transition is an induction
step and its dependency graph reaches only already-computed states. Writing the
induction is writing the correctness proof of your DP.

**Worked example: a closed form.** Let $S_n = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$, with
$S_0 = 0$. Claim: $S_n = n(n+1)/2$. At $n = 0$ both sides are $0$. Assuming it
at $n$,

$$S_{n+1} = S_n + (n+1) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (n+1) = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}.$$

Each equality is the definition, the induction hypothesis, or plain algebra —
a good proof lets the reader label every step that way.

One warning that will recur for the rest of the book: this derivation lives in
the integers and rationals, where dividing by $2$ is harmless. If you evaluate
$n(n+1)/2$ modulo $m$, divide the even factor by $2$ *before* reducing, because
$2$ may have no inverse modulo $m$ (it has none modulo $4$, for instance).
The identity is true; the naive modular translation of it is not.

**Worked example: every integer factors into primes.** A *prime* is an integer
$p \ge 2$ whose only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$. Claim: every $n \ge 2$
is a product of primes. Strong induction: if $n$ is prime we are done;
otherwise $n = ab$ with $2 \le a, b < n$, and the hypothesis factors both $a$
and $b$. Note carefully what this gives — *existence* of a factorization. That
it is *unique* is a separate and harder fact, proved below from Bézout, and
the gap between the two is not a technicality: uniqueness is what makes
"compare prime signatures" a valid algorithm.

::: {.callout-warning title="Failed induction: all objects have the same color"}
Claim: in any set of objects, all objects have the same color. Base: a
one-element set, trivially true. Step: given $n+1$ objects, the first $n$ share
a color and the last $n$ share a color, and the two groups overlap, so all
$n+1$ agree.

The conclusion is absurd, so the step must be broken — and it is, at exactly
one place. Going from $1$ to $2$, the "first $n$" and "last $n$" groups are
disjoint, so there is nothing to transfer the color through. An induction step
must be valid *at its first boundary*, not merely for comfortable large $n$.
Whenever an induction feels too easy, test the step at the very smallest index.
:::

## Invariants, potentials, and extremal choices

Many contest problems ask whether a process can reach a target state. Searching
the state space is hopeless when it is exponential; the mathematical move is to
find a quantity that *cannot change*, and observe that the start and target
disagree on it.

An **invariant** is a property preserved by every allowed transition. Proving
one takes two steps: it holds initially, and if it holds before an arbitrary
allowed move then it holds after.

A **potential function** assigns a number to a state and moves in a controlled
direction. A nonnegative *integer* potential that strictly decreases proves
termination, because a decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers is finite.
A real-valued potential that merely decreases proves nothing: $1, 1/2, 1/4,
\ldots$ decreases forever.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked example: an obstruction and a matching construction"}
A board has a $0$ or $1$ in each cell. One move picks an allowed pair of cells
and flips both.

*Obstruction.* The parity of the number of ones never changes: flipping two
cells changes the count by $-2$, $0$, or $+2$. So a board containing exactly
one $1$ can never become all zeros. This argument needed no search at all.

*Is parity enough?* Only once we say which pairs are allowed. Model cells as
vertices and allowed pairs as edges. If that graph is connected, even parity is
also sufficient: take a spanning tree, process vertices from the leaves upward,
and flip a leaf together with its parent exactly when the leaf holds a $1$. A
cleared leaf is never touched again, so the invariant "all processed vertices
are zero" is maintained. When only the root remains, it must be $0$, because
the total parity is even and everything else is zero. The construction costs
$O(V + E)$ with one traversal.

Notice the shape of the complete answer: an invariant proves that some
instances are impossible, and a construction proves that all the others are
possible. Either half alone leaves the problem unsolved.
:::

An **extremal argument** picks a smallest, largest, or otherwise most extreme
object and then exploits what that object is *unable* to do. It works because
every finite nonempty set of integers has a minimum, and — more strongly —
every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has one even if it is infinite.

**Worked example: a finite tree has a leaf.** Take a longest simple path in a
tree with at least two vertices, and look at one endpoint $u$. Could $u$ have a
neighbour besides the next vertex on the path? If that neighbour is off the
path, the path was not longest. If it is elsewhere on the path, we have a
cycle, and a tree has none. So $u$ has degree one. This is the reason that
"repeatedly strip leaves" is a legitimate induction on trees, used later in the
matrix–tree theorem in [Chapter 07](../07-linear-algebra/chapter.qmd).

## Euclid and Bézout: the first real tool

Everything in [Chapter 01](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd) rests on one
identity, so it is worth deriving rather than quoting.

For nonnegative integers $a, b$ not both zero, $g = \gcd(a,b)$ is the greatest
positive integer dividing both. Division with remainder writes $a = qb + r$
with $0 \le r < b$ whenever $b > 0$. The key observation is that an integer
divides both $a$ and $b$ exactly when it divides both $b$ and $r = a - qb$:
each of $a$ and $r$ is an integer combination of the other pair. The two pairs
therefore have the *same set of common divisors*, hence the same greatest one:

$$\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, r).$$

The remainders strictly decrease and stay nonnegative, so the process stops —
a potential-function argument — and the last nonzero remainder is $g$. That is
Euclid's algorithm, and the proof above is the whole of its correctness.

Now track a little more information. Every remainder produced along the way is
an integer combination $au + bv$ of the original inputs: this is true of the
starting values ($a = a\cdot 1 + b \cdot 0$ and $b = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1$),
and subtracting $q$ times one combination from another produces a combination
again. Since $g$ is one of the remainders, there exist integers $u, v$ with

$$au + bv = g.$$

This is **Bézout's identity**, and the running bookkeeping of $(u,v)$ is
exactly what the extended Euclidean algorithm returns.

**Small instance.** For $a = 30$, $b = 18$: the remainders are $12$, then $6$,
then $0$, so $g = 6$. Back-substituting, $6 = 18 - 12 = 18 - (30 - 18) =
2 \cdot 18 - 30$. Hence $30x + 18y = 6$ has the solution $(x,y) = (-1, 2)$.

**When is $ax + by = c$ solvable, and what are all the solutions?** Solvable
exactly when $g \mid c$. Necessity is immediate: $g$ divides every value the
left-hand side can take. Sufficiency: multiply Bézout's coefficients by $c/g$.
And when $a, b > 0$, every solution is obtained from a single solution
$(x_0, y_0)$ as

$$x = x_0 + \frac{b}{g}t, \qquad y = y_0 - \frac{a}{g}t, \qquad t \in \mathbb Z.$$

Why are there no others? Subtract two solutions to get
$(a/g)\,\Delta x = -(b/g)\,\Delta y$. The integers $a/g$ and $b/g$ are coprime,
so $b/g$ divides $\Delta x$ — this is Bézout again — which is precisely the
parameterization above. Degenerate coefficients are handled directly; if both
$a$ and $b$ are zero, the equation is solvable exactly when $c = 0$.

This completeness statement is what contest problems actually need. They rarely
ask for *a* solution; they ask for the smallest nonnegative one, or for the
number of solutions in a window, and those questions are answered by the
parameter $t$, not by whatever pair extended Euclid happened to return.

**Cost.** Euclid performs $O(\log \max(a,b))$ divisions on positive inputs,
because the larger argument at least halves every two steps. That counts
arithmetic operations; on big integers each division has its own bit cost.

::: {.callout-note title="Why prime factorization is unique"}
Suppose a prime $p$ divides $ab$ but not $a$. Then $\gcd(p,a) = 1$, so Bézout
gives $pu + av = 1$. Multiply by $b$:

$$pub + abv = b.$$

Both terms on the left are divisible by $p$ — the first visibly, the second
because $p \mid ab$ — so $p \mid b$. Hence a prime dividing a product divides
one of the factors.

Uniqueness follows: a prime appearing in one factorization of $n$ must appear
in any other, so cancel it from both and repeat. Two factorizations of the same
integer therefore agree up to order.
:::

## Double counting and bijections

The last foundational habit is the one that makes combinatorics feel like
programming rather than memorization: before rearranging a sum, name the
objects its terms count. Then, if you can count the same collection a second
way, the two answers must agree — and you have proved an identity without any
algebra at all.

**The handshake identity.** In a finite undirected graph, count *incidences*:
pairs $(v, e)$ where $v$ is an endpoint of edge $e$. Group by vertex and you
get $\sum_v \deg(v)$. Group by edge and you get $2|E|$, since each edge has two
endpoints. The two totals count one set, so they are equal. (With self-loops,
define degree by counting endpoint occurrences, and the statement survives.)

**Binomial coefficients from a bijection.** Let $\binom{n}{k}$ be the number of
$k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set; it is $0$ when $k < 0$ or $k > n$.
Count ordered lists of $k$ distinct elements directly:
$n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ choices. Now count them a second way: choose the
underlying subset, then order it, which is $\binom{n}{k} \cdot k!$ lists. Hence

$$\binom nk = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}, \qquad 0 \le k \le n,$$

where $n!$ is the product of $1$ through $n$ and $0! = 1$. The division is
exact over the integers — the left side counts things. Over a modulus it needs
its own justification, which is the subject of
[Chapter 04](../04-modular-binomials/chapter.qmd).

Splitting on whether one distinguished element is in the subset gives Pascal's
recurrence $\binom nk = \binom{n-1}{k} + \binom{n-1}{k-1}$ for $n \ge 1$: the
subsets avoiding the element, plus the subsets using it.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked example: a team and its captain"}
From $n \ge 1$ people, choose a nonempty team and designate one member as
captain. How many outcomes?

*Count by team size.* A team of size $k$ can be chosen in $\binom nk$ ways and
has $k$ captain choices, giving $\sum_{k=1}^{n} k \binom nk$.

*Count by captain first.* Pick the captain: $n$ ways. Each of the remaining
$n-1$ people independently joins or does not: $2^{n-1}$ ways.

Both describe the same outcomes, so

$$\sum_{k} k \binom nk = n\,2^{n-1}.$$

Check at $n = 3$: the left side is $1\cdot3 + 2\cdot3 + 3\cdot1 = 12$, and the
right side is $3 \cdot 4 = 12$. Note that the $2^{n-1}$ counts *subsets* of the
remaining people, not orderings of them — mixing up those two is the most
common way a double count goes wrong.
:::

## Contest translation and checklist

Use a library routine only after your reduction has a written contract: what
goes in, what comes out, and under what hypotheses. Keep four separate claims
straight, because they fail in different ways:

1. the model faithfully describes the problem;
2. every valid solution is represented in the model (nothing is lost);
3. the algorithm returns the quantity actually asked for;
4. the resource bound fits the constraints.

A brute-force comparison on small inputs can *refute* any of the four, which
makes it extremely worthwhile. It can never establish them for arbitrary
inputs, which is why the derivation still has to exist.

Before coding, answer:

- What is the domain, including the empty case, zero, and the boundary of every
  range?
- Is my condition necessary, sufficient, or both — and which do I need?
- Which concrete object does one summand, or one DP state, represent?
- What is preserved by a transition, and what guarantees termination?
- When I divide a count by a symmetry factor, are all the groups really the
  same size?
- Does my complexity count arithmetic operations or actual machine work on
  numbers of this size?

## Exercises, hints, and solutions

### 1. Quantifiers and a counterexample — concept check

Negate the statement "every pair of nonzero residues modulo $m$ has a nonzero
product". Then find the smallest $m \ge 2$ for which the original statement is
false.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* the negation asserts the existence of a bad pair; look for a modulus
that factors.

The negation is: "there exist two nonzero residues modulo $m$ whose product is
zero." Modulo $2$ and modulo $3$, multiplying out all pairs shows no such pair
exists. Modulo $4$, $2 \cdot 2 = 0$. The answer is $m = 4$.

This is the first appearance of the theme that dominates
[Chapter 01](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd): *nonzero does not mean
invertible.* Modulo $4$, the residue $2$ is nonzero yet has no reciprocal, so
any derivation that "divides by $2$" there is invalid.
:::

### 2. Count the same marked subset twice — derivation

For $n \ge 2$, derive $\sum_{k=0}^{n} k(k-1)\binom nk = n(n-1)2^{\,n-2}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* mimic the team-and-captain count, but mark an ordered pair.

Count pairs consisting of a subset together with an ordered pair of two
distinct chosen members.

By subset size: a $k$-element subset admits $k(k-1)$ ordered pairs, giving the
left-hand side.

By marked pair first: choose the ordered pair in $n(n-1)$ ways, then let each
of the remaining $n-2$ people independently join or not, giving $2^{n-2}$.

Both count the same objects, so the identity holds. Check at $n = 3$: the left
side is $2 \cdot 3 + 6 \cdot 1 = 12$ and the right side is $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 =
12$.
:::

### 3. All bounded solutions — modelling

Find every pair of nonnegative integers with $6x + 9y = 45$ and $x \le 6$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* divide by the gcd first, then use the full parameterization rather than
stopping at one solution.

Since $\gcd(6,9) = 3$ divides $45$, solutions exist; dividing through gives
$2x + 3y = 15$. One solution is $(0,5)$, and the general one is $x = 3t$,
$y = 5 - 2t$.

Now impose the constraints: $y \ge 0$ gives $t \le 2$, and $x \ge 0$ with
$x \le 6$ gives $0 \le t \le 2$. The pairs are $(0,5)$, $(3,3)$, $(6,1)$.

Guessing a single solution would have reported one pair out of three. The
parameterization is what makes the enumeration complete.
:::

### 4. Flip graph on a disconnected board — synthesis

Extend the two-cell flip model to an allowed-pair graph that may be
disconnected. State a necessary and sufficient condition for reaching the
all-zero state, and give a construction.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
*Hint:* a move never crosses between components, so each component carries its
own invariant.

Every move flips two endpoints of one edge, so it stays inside a single
connected component; the parity of ones is therefore invariant *per component*.
Hence even parity in every component is necessary.

It is also sufficient: apply the spanning-tree leaf procedure independently in
each component. An isolated vertex is its own component with no edges, so it
must already hold $0$ — its parity condition says exactly that.

Total cost is $O(V+E)$, with at most $V - 1$ flips across all components. The
answer combines an obstruction with a matching construction, which is strictly
stronger than either half.
:::

## Summary and reference sheet

- An implication needs one direction; an equivalence needs two, and reductions
  almost always need two.
- Negating a quantified claim tells you what a counterexample looks like — and
  therefore what your brute-force checker should hunt for.
- Induction needs a valid base *and* a step that works at the first boundary.
  Strong induction is the proof form of a dynamic program.
- An invariant proves impossibility; a construction proves possibility; a
  complete answer usually needs both.
- A strictly decreasing nonnegative integer potential proves termination. A
  decreasing real quantity does not.
- Euclid: $\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$. Bézout: $au + bv = \gcd(a,b)$.
  Hence $ax + by = c$ is solvable exactly when $\gcd(a,b) \mid c$, and all
  solutions form the one-parameter family above.
- A prime dividing a product divides a factor; this is why prime factorizations
  are unique.
- A bijection or a double count proves an equality by describing one finite
  collection in two ways. Factorial division is exact over the integers and
  needs separate justification over a modulus.

Continue with [modular algebra](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd), where
Bézout immediately becomes the theory of division modulo $m$. Later,
[combinatorics](../03-combinatorics/chapter.qmd),
[linear algebra](../07-linear-algebra/chapter.qmd), and
[probability](../12-probability/chapter.qmd) build their own objects on the
same foundations.
